## TL;DR

Added a purpose-built Work queue for viewports below the shared 720 px responsive boundary. Mobile Work now presents a vertical list of readable, wrapping task cards with status filtering, updated-time ordering, a visible reset action, and a touch-sized New task button. The existing board remains the desktop composition and continues to use the same task store and creation drawer. Focused UI coverage passes across cards, loading and empty states, filter exhaustion, refresh retry, create flow, and desktop composition.

## Work and rationale

The implementation follows the mobile direction already established by ADR 0011 and the completed shell work in #1112. `WorkView.vue` now selects a separate `MobileWorkQueue` component when `useResponsiveLayout()` reports a narrow viewport. This keeps the desktop board’s multi-column markup intact on wide screens and ensures the mobile list is not a CSS reflow of `BoardColumn` or `TaskCard`. The page boundary comes from the shared matchMedia composable, so resizing and rotation use the same 720 px rule as the mobile navigation shell.

The new component reads `repo.tasks` and `repo.loading` directly from the active Pinia store. Its computed list excludes archived and held tasks, applies an optional canonical status filter, then sorts by `updated_at` in either direction. Newest first is the initial order. Filter and sort state live in the component, which makes the Reset control a simple and visible return to the complete queue without adding URL or persisted preference behavior to this narrow feature.

Each task is a full-width button with a separate number and update timestamp line, a wrapping title, and compact type, priority, and status labels. The full card opens the current task through `ui.openTask`, preserving the existing task detail behavior. The prominent New task button calls `ui.openNewTask()` and therefore enters the same drawer and shared task mutation flow as desktop. The empty queue offers that creation action again; filtered-empty content gives the user a direct way to clear the selection.

For recoverable network failures, the queue exposes a Retry button that calls `repo.refresh()`, the store’s existing board-index refresh path. It shows the returned error inline and prevents duplicate requests while the retry is in flight. Initial application loading remains owned by the app shell/store; the component also understands `repo.loading` for cases where it is mounted while the shared store is still loading. Task creation and ongoing task updates are not duplicated or reimplemented in the mobile view.

Styling is local to the mobile component. It uses the existing theme variables, restrained borders, text wrapping, visible keyboard focus, and controls with touch-appropriate height. The control row is a grid with min-width constraints so narrow labels and long task titles wrap inside the viewport. No hover is required to reveal a queue action. The desktop view is still selected above the breakpoint and its prior board controls and markup remain within the existing branch.

## Approaches tried

I inspected the task specification, ADR 0011, the #1112 task contract, the existing Work view, shared responsive composable, task store, date formatter, and new-task drawer entry points. I chose a separate routed-view child component instead of adding mobile branches inside `TaskCard` or `BoardColumn`: those desktop components contain board-specific interaction density and would make the narrow composition harder to keep structurally independent.

The filter uses the repository’s styled select primitives, while updated-time sort is a compact toggle. This keeps the control set small and avoids introducing a native select or a second sorting model in the store. Status filtering and the sort toggle are intentionally local view state; the queue resets visibly to all statuses and newest updates.

I added component-level tests using a real Pinia store and light UI stubs. The tests verify rendered card information, loading and no-task content, filtered-empty direction, network failure and a successful refresh retry, the existing new-task action, and the wide-screen Work board path. During the first run, the fixture’s default loading state hid a card, the button stub invoked handlers twice, and the desktop view lacked its router injection. I corrected those test harness issues rather than changing production behavior to accommodate them.

## Challenges and blockers

The key boundary was distinguishing the desktop board’s existing data and mutation behavior from its DOM. The mobile composition needed enough functionality to be useful without pulling the desktop board controls and card action surface into a narrow layout. A separate component made that boundary explicit while keeping shared store state and actions.

The shared store handles its initial load at the app shell, so a standalone retry affordance is most useful after a refresh request fails. The mobile view reports that failure and retries through `repo.refresh()`. It does not invent a second transport client or a parallel task cache. The integration test confirms the store calls the existing `/api/board` endpoint on retry.

No human account, device, or server-session work was needed. A real-device overflow audit was not performed during this implementation; the coverage checks structural behavior and the layout uses bounded grid columns, wrapping text, and zero-width-safe flex/grid children. The UI build and scoped RepoOS verification are the final technical gates for this branch.

## Key learnings

The existing responsive composable is already shared by the shell and is the right boundary for routed page compositions. Work task creation is also already cleanly centralized in the UI store and repo store, allowing the new mobile queue to remain a presentation layer rather than acquire its own mutation path.

The Work board’s current `repo.tasks` collection can power a distinct list directly, while the store’s `refresh()` method provides a suitable recovery path for network errors. The date helper `relTime` supplies concise updated-time labels without custom timestamp logic. For this feature, independent composition plus shared state produces a simpler mobile surface and preserves desktop behavior with only a small view-selection change.
